title: A 62mW Stereo Class-G Headphone Driver with 108dB Dynamic Range and 600μA/Channel Quiescent Current Jianlong Chen1, Sasi Kumar Arunachalam1, Todd L. Brooks1, Iuri Mehr1, Felix Cheung1, Hariprasath Venkatram2
figure_number: Figure 10.6.3 shows the overall headphone driver architecture. Headphone drivers usually need a high-order loop filter to suppress non-linearity and power supply disturbance from the output stage [1][2]. Taking advantage of the high gain associated with the adaptive class-B control scheme, a simple first-order loop filter is sufficient to suppress non-linearity and battery power supply variation. Part of the variation is due to the class-G operation. When the output voltage rises above a threshold, the supply for the driver output stage is increased. If the output voltage is below the threshold, the supply is reduced in an efficient way, using a charge pump (class-G supply as shown in Fig. 10.6.3). A first-order Gm-C filter is used as loop filter. The transconductance cell is implemented as a low-noise, high voltage gain input stage followed by a 1/R second stage to reduce the overall Gm value. Hence, the overall Gm is defined by the input differential pair (transistors M1/M2) gm divided by R2/R1 ratio.
